title: My shop lot has tripled in value but is hard to rent. Should I sell?
excerpt: A 41-year-old's paid-off Butterworth shop lot, bought for RM240,000, has an RM800,000 offer but half of it sits empty. Sean says hold for now, check the real value and rent, and pay someone to manage it.

question.asker: From R, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: R, 41, lives in the Klang Valley with a young child and has no debts. At 26 she bought a shop lot in Butterworth for about RM240,000, with her parents paying a RM100,000 down payment; it is now fully paid. The ground floor is let for RM1,200 a month to a good tenant who threatened to leave when she proposed a RM200 increase, the upper floor has never found a tenant, and her ageing father handles repairs and viewings. Someone has offered RM800,000; she also has about RM400,000 in shares and the rest in fixed deposits.
question.text: Should she sell the shop lot or keep it, and if she sells, what should she buy in the Klang Valley?

answer.quote: I will only sell if I am certain there is another better deal.
answer.summary: Hold it for now. It costs almost nothing to keep, protects her money against inflation and can be refinanced in an emergency. Check its real value and the going rent, pay a contractor or property manager instead of relying on her father, and only sell when a clearly better deal comes along.

reasons.title: Get the facts first
reasons.body: Ask a bank for a valuation to see whether RM800,000 is fair, and check rents for similar shop lots nearby. If the area rents for more than RM1,200, the tenant's threat to leave carries less weight.

reasons.title: Cash in the bank loses ground
reasons.body: Her RM100,000 down payment 15 years ago was worth far more than RM100,000 today. Sold for RM800,000 with nowhere to put it, the cash would at best hold its value while prices keep rising.

reasons.title: Refinancing keeps the asset
reasons.body: If she needs money, refinancing takes about four to five months against six to eight for a sale, and she keeps the shop lot. Commercial loans usually cover about 70% to 80%.

reasons.title: Sell for something better
reasons.body: For example, a RM2 million Penang shop lot renting for about RM8,000 a month: with RM800,000 down, the RM1.4 million loan would cost about RM5,600 to RM6,000 a month, which the rent covers. A deal like that justifies selling.

actions: Ask a bank to value the shop lot and compare with the RM800,000 offer.
Check rents for similar units nearby before renewing the tenancy.
Hire a reliable contractor or property manager for repairs and viewings.
Learn the Klang Valley market separately: watch reviews and view about 20 properties.
Sell only if you find a deal whose rent covers its loan and beats what the shop lot gives you.
caveat: Commercial loans have lower margins and need more cash upfront than residential ones. If she simply doesn't want the hassle of a property far away, selling is a reasonable choice once she knows its true value.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #210. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in April 2023.
